title: Investigating Attention Contagion Between Students in a Lecture Hall cture-hall/ -- original paper: https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-18528-001
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Forrin, Kudsi, Cyr, Sana, Davidesco and Kim's study investigating whether attentiveness spreads contagiously between students seated together in a physical lecture hall, extending earlier online-classroom findings to face-to-face teaching. Researchers planted attentive or inattentive confederates among real students and varied seating proximity to test the effect on onlookers' attentiveness, note-taking, and quiz performance. The key finding is asymmetric: inattentiveness spread contagiously between students, but attentiveness did not, and the effect was strongest for students seated between two inattentive peers. Students who caught this contagious inattention took fewer notes and scored worse on a subsequent content quiz. Mediation analyses point to two social mechanisms — goal contagion and social appraisal of how important the lecture seems — as partial explanations, echoing the mechanisms found in the earlier online-classroom research. Barton draws out the seating-plan implication directly: instinctively placing distracting students at the back doesn't neutralise the contagion risk, and seating an inattentive student in the middle of a device-free room can still drag down the attentiveness of those around them.
points: The contagion effect is asymmetric — inattentiveness spreads between students, but attentiveness does not, meaning teachers have more to lose from a visibly disengaged student than to gain from a visibly engaged one.

Effects hold even in a device-free classroom, which rules out phone/screen visibility as the sole mechanism and implicates purely social processes — goal contagion and social appraisal of the lecture's importance.
Contagious inattention has a measurable academic cost: affected students took fewer notes and performed worse on a subsequent quiz, not just a subjective 'feeling' of distraction.
Seating position matters more than intuition suggests — placing an inattentive student in the middle of the room, not just at the back, can spread disengagement to the peers seated around them.

Barton frames the practical takeaway as proactive classroom management: actively monitoring and addressing inattentiveness, and building a culture where attentiveness feels normal and expected, blunts the contagion before it spreads.
quotes: This research article investigates attention contagion in a university lecture hall. Researchers manipulated student attentiveness (attentive vs. inattentive confederates) and seating proximity to examine its impact on participants' attentiveness, note-taking, and quiz performance.
The study found that inattentiveness, but not attentiveness, spread contagiously, particularly among students seated between inattentive peers.

Inattention is contagious. Students are more likely to become inattentive themselves if they see their classmates being inattentive. This was especially true when students were seated between inattentive peers.
Inattention contagion can negatively impact learning. The study found that students who became inattentive due to their peers took fewer notes and performed worse on a quiz about the lecture.

Even in a device-free classroom, inattentive behavior can spread from student to student. This suggests that other factors, like goal contagion and social appraisals of lecture importance, are also at play.
While it may seem intuitive to seat distracting students at the back, in a device-free classroom, seating inattentive students in the middle may negatively affect those around them.

Instructors and students should be aware that inattention spreads during lectures, even in device-free classrooms, and meaningfully affects learning and academic performance. Inattention is contagious.
